It specifies that the integral over $[-σ, σ]$ is twice the size of the integral outside this interval (due to symmetry and the nature of the derivative), and that the CDF is scaled such that it equals $1/2$ at $τ_i = -σ$ (noting that the text contains a typo '41' which contextually and mathematically refers to $1/2$, consistent with the piecewise definition provided where the middle term is $1/2 + ...$). It builds on the work of Fischer and Ritschel [7] who derived 1D Gaussian gradient sampling, but extends it to $n$-dimensions via marginalization [S1].

The claim states that the work builds on Fischer and Ritschel [7] who derived 1D Gaussian gradient sampling, and extends it to n-dimensions via marginalization. Source [S1] explicitly states in Section B: 'The sampling of 1D Gaussian gradient was derived by Fischer and Ritschel [7]... For an n-dimensional Gaussian gradient, we need to marginalize and sample the dimensions individually.' It further contrasts this with Fischer and Ritschel [7] who 'only blur in the direction in which they differentiate,' whereas the current method blurs all dimensions. This confirms both the basis on Fischer and Ritschel's 1D work and the extension to n-dimensions via marginalization.

Smooth Gradient Marginalization is a technique to sample an $n$-dimensional Gaussian gradient by marginalizing the probability density function (PDF) over all dimensions except the one being differentiated, allowing individual dimension sampling [S1].

The claim states that Smooth Gradient Marginalization is a technique to sample an n-dimensional Gaussian gradient by marginalizing the PDF over all dimensions except the one being differentiated, allowing individual dimension sampling. Source [S1], specifically Section B titled 'Smooth Gradient Marginalization', explicitly states: 'For an n-dimensional Gaussian gradient, we need to marginalize and sample the dimensions individually. Marginalization would be integration over all dimensions j != i, except the one we look for i'. This matches the claim exactly.

Since the Gaussian is separable, $N(\tau) = \prod_{j=1}^n N(\tau_j)$, the integration over all $N(\tau_j)$ for $j \neq i$ evaluates to 1, leaving the magnitude of the 1D gradient [S1].

The claim states that because the Gaussian is separable, the integration over all dimensions $j$ except $i$ evaluates to 1, leaving the magnitude of the 1D gradient. Source [S1] explicitly supports this in Section B ('Smooth Gradient Marginalization'). Specifically, Equation (32) shows the integral of the product of 1D Gaussians. Equation (33) states 'As we differentiate only by $	au_i$, all other factors are 1'. Equation (34) concludes 'As we are integrating over all $	au_{j ackslash i}$, integration becomes multiplication with the domain’s measure, 1', resulting in the term $|	abla_i N(	au_i)|$ (the magnitude of the 1D gradient). Thus, every fact in the claim is present and supported by the evidence.
supported

A critical distinction is that the diagonal element is not a special case of the off-diagonal element because the variable appears twice in the differentiation ($d(u^2)/du = 2u$ vs $d(uv)/du = v$) [S1].

The claim states that the diagonal element is not a special case of the off-diagonal element because the variable appears twice in the differentiation, citing the examples $d(u^2)/du = 2u$ vs $d(uv)/du = v$. Source [S1] explicitly contains a remark stating: 'It might appear, that diagonal is a special case of off-diagonal, but for differentiation, that is not true, as on the diagonal, the variable we differentiate in respect to appears twice, in the sense that duv/du = v and duv/dv = u, but duu/du = 2u.' This matches the claim exactly.
